annotations.text: 375 — two things leave the stage. The phone silhouette goes, because she is already holding one and drawing a phone inside a phone is a picture of a picture. The photography plate goes too; at 327px it would be a stamp, so the photograph returns further down the page as the section's own image. The thread plays straight on the field and the cards resolve beneath a hairline. CTA is full width at 56px.

768 — the two hero columns stack. Copy keeps a 560px measure instead of running the full width, so the headline breaks in two lines and the lead stays inside 52 characters. The stage drops below it and is actually wider here than on laptop — 672px against 564 — so the cards spread into the extra room rather than the phone growing. Nav collapses to wordmark, Start a gift, and a two-rule menu.

1280 — same asymmetric 5 / 6 split as 1440, margins at 64, stage 520 tall. Nothing reflows here; it is the same layout at a tighter measure. If the two widths looked different from each other, one of them would be wrong.

1440+ — 12 columns, 96px margins. Copy sits in columns 1–5, the stage in 7–12, so a whole empty column separates them. That gap is the most expensive thing on the page. Content caps at 1440 and centres beyond it; the ground colour runs edge to edge.

Copy is the brief's, verbatim, with three design decisions on top:

— "for her" is set in the serif's italic. It is the only italic in the hero, and it puts the weight on the person rather than the product.
— The moss eyebrow is the one place the second accent appears above the fold.
— "She did none of it." sits under the resolved cards. Four words carrying the whole proposition, in her voice, in the serif.

One primary action only. "Start a gift" stays a quiet text link in the nav so "See the gift" is unopposed.

What every hero shows in the stage is frame 09 — the animation's rest state, which is also the poster image and the reduced-motion still.

The stage is composed to stand with no photograph in it: window light from the upper left, 5.5% film grain, and the thread bleeding off the bottom edge so the frame reads as a crop rather than a box. Shot 01 drops in full-bleed behind it when the shoot lands. The art direction for that shoot is the artboard to the right.

Nine frames, 14.0 seconds, reading left to right in three rows. Each frame shows the state at the END of its beat, not the transition into it — the transition is written in the Motion row beneath.

The three columns inside every frame stay fixed: the photography plate, her thread, and the things around her. The storyboard keeps the plate as its own column so each beat stays readable; in the built hero the photograph sits full-bleed behind the other two. Nothing ever moves between columns. The whole piece is one idea — the right-hand column resolving while she does almost nothing.

Frame 09 is the hero's poster frame, card for card and bubble for bubble. If either changes, both change.

This is the set the hero establishes, and it is meant to be the whole set. Ten colours, two families, three easing curves, four durations, two shadows, three radii, one stagger value.

Every later section — data forward, care balance, the package open state, the six flow steps — is built from exactly this and nothing added. If a section needs a new token, the section is wrong.

Commissioned, not stocked. Every stock library's “new mother” is the exact thing this brand exists to be the opposite of, and one wrong frame undoes the whole palette.

The constraint that matters most is in shot 01: the right half of the frame must be empty room, because the resolved cards live there. That is layout, not styling — if it is not shot that way the hero does not assemble.
